hints: Notice the slow vehicle and fast vehicle are moving towards each other, so choose one direction as positive and write total momentum as a difference.
Connect the collision forces to impulse: each vehicle receives an impulse opposite to its own initial velocity, tending to reduce its forward momentum.
Compare kinetic energy before and after: a passive collision cannot create extra kinetic energy to make the already fast vehicle move even faster in the same direction.
walkthrough: Take the fast vehicle's initial direction as positive. The slow vehicle then has negative velocity, so total momentum is $p = m_{fast}v_{fast} - m_{slow}v_{slow}$.
During contact, Newton's third law gives equal and opposite forces. The impulse on the fast vehicle is opposite to its motion, so its forward momentum must decrease.

Total momentum is conserved and kinetic energy cannot increase in a normal collision between the vehicles, so any loss of forward momentum by the fast vehicle is shared as rebound or motion of the other vehicle.
The slow vehicle can be stopped and then driven backward, so its speed measured as magnitude can end up larger than before, especially if hit by a massive fast vehicle.
The fast vehicle cannot keep its direction and end with larger magnitude of velocity, because that would require a forward impulse and extra kinetic energy regardless of masses. This is option C

options.A: Both stopping is possible if the opposite momenta cancel, with $m_{slow}v_{slow} = m_{fast}v_{fast}$.
options.B: One vehicle stopping while the other rebounds is possible for suitable mass and speed combinations.
options.C: The collision impulse opposes the fast vehicle's motion, so it must slow down or at most rebound, and cannot gain speed without extra energy input.
options.D: The slow vehicle can be pushed backward by the fast vehicle and rebound with larger speed.
